cards.explanation: The answer is True. A man shows up from Saul's camp with torn clothes and dust on his head, and when he reaches David he falls to the ground to pay him homage. I walk into a room and trip over the rug. He walked in and went down on purpose.

The answer is that they fled from the battle. The man says, “The troops fled from the battle…” and many of them fell and died. Then comes the part that lands hardest, that Saul, Israel's king, and his son Jonathan are dead too. This is a heavy piece of news, friends, and I think David felt every word of it.

The answer is an Amalekite. When Saul asks who he is, the man says he told him, “I am an Amalekite.” Verse 1 says David had just come back from the slaughter of the Amalekites. So that's who is standing in front of David with this news.

The answer is agony, and it's a hard word. The man says Saul begged him, “Stand over me and kill me, for agony has seized me, but my life still lingers.” That's the man's version of the story, told to David. I think this is one of the heavy parts, so we'll just let it sit.

The answer is his crown and armband. The man says, “…I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.” He says he brought them to David. That's what he says he took from Saul.

The answer is True. David takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and “…all the men who were with him did the same.” His men tore their clothes right along with him. Verse 12 says they mourned and wept and fasted until evening.

The answer is False. The text says they mourned “…for Saul and his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.” So it wasn't only those two. They wept and fasted until evening for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel too.

The answer is that David asks why he wasn't afraid to kill God's chosen king. David says, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” That's how David describes Saul, as the LORD’s anointed. It's a sharp question from a man who had just been mourning.

The answer is execute. David summons one of the young men and says, “Go, execute him!” He's speaking about the Amalekite who said he killed Saul. It's a serious moment, friends. I think we just let it be what it is.

The answer is the sons of Judah. David “…ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow.” That's the name of the lament, and it's written in the Book of Jashar. Verse 17 says David took up this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan. He wanted it learned, not just sung once and forgotten.

The answer is so the Philistines won't rejoice. David sings, “Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” Gath and Ashkelon are the places he names. He asks that it not be told there, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice.

The answer is True. David sings, “O mountains of Gilboa, may you have no dew or rain, no fields yielding offerings of grain. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled…” That's the reason in the song. Saul's shield is named right there too, “…no longer anointed with oil.”
The answer is False. The song says, “…the sword of Saul did not return empty.” Right before it, Jonathan's bow “…did not retreat…” David sings a good word about both of them.

The answer is that they were not divided. David sings, “Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death.” Saul, Israel's king, and Jonathan, his son, are named together here. David puts them side by side in the song.

The answer is that he dressed them in scarlet and gold. David sings to weep for Saul, “…who clothed you in scarlet and luxury, who decked your garments with ornaments of gold.” That's a wardrobe upgrade, friends. Notice David is the one calling the daughters of Israel to weep.
The answer is brother. David sings, “I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother.” Jonathan is Saul's son, and here David speaks right to him. It's the song getting personal.
The answer is True. David sings to Jonathan, “You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary…” Those are David's own words about his friend. He doesn't hold back.
